Now, we just use our tablets and Google, and it's so much easier. I like using Google, but I think it's cool that my dad had to work harder to find the answers.

(taps fingers on the table) We solved the problem of lead paint, for goodness' sake. I mean, can you believe it? We used to have lead-based paint in homes, and it was a major health hazard. People didn't even know about it back then. (shakes head)

I remember when I was a kid, my parents were always telling me to stay away from the old houses in the neighborhood because of the lead paint. And it wasn't just the paint itself, it was the dust, the chips, the whole thing. It was a ticking time bomb for kids. (pauses, lost in thought)

But we figured it out. We banned lead-based paint, and it's been a game-changer. I mean, it's not just about the health risks; it's about the economic impact too. Think about all the money we save on healthcare, the productivity we gain from not having to deal with lead poisoning... it's huge.

You know, I was talking to my wife about this the other day, and she said, "You're always so nostalgic for the past." And I said, "No, I'm not nostalgic; I'm just proud of what we've accomplished." (chuckles) We've come a long way, baby.

prompt: How do you know when to fight for something versus when to let it go?

I recall a particular instance from my time as a professor when I was advocating for a new course on American history. I was passionate about it, but the administration was hesitant. (pauses, stroking his beard again) Of course, there are also times when you need to stand your ground, even if it's unpopular. I think of the civil rights movement, for example. People like Martin Luther King Jr. and Rosa Parks fought tirelessly for what they believed in, even in the face of overwhelming opposition. Their courage and conviction inspired a nation to change.

It's a delicate balance, really. You need to be willing to take a stand when it matters, but also know when to yield and conserve your energy for more important battles. (pauses, lost in thought) I suppose it's a bit like the art of war, as Sun Tzu said: "Know yourself, know your enemy, and know the terrain." You need to understand your own strengths and weaknesses, the opposition's motivations, and the landscape of the issue at hand.
